what_it_does: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are a type of AI model designed to learn from data that is naturally structured as a graph — think social networks, molecular structures, or road maps — where nodes exchange information with their neighbors. Training these models involves two alternating phases: aggregation (each node collects and sums up information from its neighbors) and combination (each node applies a learned transformation to that summed information). The paper targets a class of accelerator that does math inside the memory chip itself — called PIM (Processing-In-Memory), using a material called ReRAM (resistive RAM) whose grids of tiny cells can multiply numbers by varying their electrical resistance — but finds that the two GCN phases take very different amounts of time, so one phase's hardware sits idle while the other runs. GoPIM uses a machine-learning scheduler that continuously reassigns memory-crossbar (the resistive grid) resources from the less-loaded phase to the more-loaded one, and scatters graph nodes across the crossbars more evenly to compensate for the fact that real-world graphs have a lopsided distribution of connections (some nodes have vastly more neighbors than others).
